title: Count the cost (Luke 14:25–35)
hookLine: a builder counts the cost before starting a tower

cards: Plenty of towns have one: a building started and never finished. Concrete pillars with rusting rods sticking out the top, a fence around it, weeds growing through the foundation. Locals give it a nickname.
Drive past, and the thought comes on its own: somebody ran out of money. Jesus uses that same picture at a moment you might not expect, when great crowds are following him down the road.

teach.b: Luke says great multitudes went with him, and he turned and spoke to them, not to thank the crowd but to slow it down.
First a hard saying: whoever comes to him and does not hate father and mother, even their own life, cannot be his disciple. It sounds shocking, and it should be heard carefully.

teach.h: HATE: A BIBLE WAY TO SAY LOVE LESS.
teach.b: In the Bible's own way of speaking, hate can mean love less, put second. Genesis says Leah was hated, when the story has just said Jacob loved Rachel more.

Matthew gives the same saying plainly: "He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." Read that way, Jesus isn't asking anyone to despise their family; he's saying nothing can come before him.
Then the picture: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?"
Otherwise you lay the foundation, can't finish, and everyone who sees it begins to mock you: "This man began to build, and was not able to finish."

Then a king with ten thousand soldiers facing one with twenty thousand: he sits down first, and counts. Notice the word sits, twice. Discipleship here isn't a rush of feeling at the back of a big crowd.

teach.h: THIS MAN BEGAN TO BUILD, AND WAS NOT ABLE TO FINISH.
teach.b: It's a decision made sitting down, with the numbers in front of you. And Jesus doesn't hide the total. Luke ends the passage plainly: whoever does not forsake all that he has cannot be his disciple.

how: Some churches ask adults to prepare over weeks or months before baptism, confirmation or membership, and religious orders give long periods of testing before final vows, so people can count the cost first.

o: the Bible's first book, with Jacob, Leah and Rachel
the book where the law is given at Sinai
the book of the Gospels about Jesus' birth

games.q: what's inside Luke 14:25–35 — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus is asking his followers to despise their families
hate here can mean love less, as with Leah and Rachel; Matthew has "loveth father or mother more than me."
Jesus spoke about counting the cost to a large crowd
great multitudes went with him, and he turned and told them to sit down and count.
the king in the story sits down first to count
ten thousand against twenty thousand: he sits down first and consults.

games.q: great crowds are following you down the road. what do you say to them?
o: sit down first and count what this will cost you.
games.why: Jesus turns and tells them about the tower and the king: count the cost first, because it may be everything.

practice: Sit down like the builder and choose one thing you've said yes to, or are about to: a job, a relationship, a promise to volunteer, a faith practice like this one.
Count it honestly, item by item, in time, money, energy and what you'll give up, without letting yourself off with a vague answer. Then ask: can I finish this tower?

wordCard.voice: Genesis. The book where love held second is called hate, the Hebrew way of speaking behind Jesus's hard saying that whoever will not count this cost cannot be his disciple.

orig.note: Greek: counts, reckons. the builder's verb in 14:28; the King James Bible says counteth.

carryVoice: Your line: can I finish this tower? The builder sits down before he builds. See you tomorrow.
